metadata.title: On iki Sözcüğü Geçmeyen Başlık 16 Punto İlk Harfleri Büyük, Ortalı ve Kalın Yazınız
metadata.venue: Journal of Measurement and Evaluation in Education and Psychology

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 Türkiye student microdata (15-year-olds in formal secondary education) and restricts the dataset to student questionnaire variables only (excluding school and parent questionnaires). The authors report that OECD-provided student weights exist to address nonresponse and unequal selection probabilities, but they also state that complex sampling weights could not be fully integrated into predictive models because PISA’s complex sampling design is not straightforward to incorporate into the machine-learning workflow. Therefore, the modeling is described as unweighted within the 10-fold cross-validation pipeline, while preprocessing (missingness trimming, missForest imputation, 5% trimming of outliers, and re-standardization within Türkiye) is applied prior to model training. As a result, generalizability is framed as limited to the national level rather than fully design-representative estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Starting from 7,250 Turkish students in PISA 2022, cases with more than 30% missing data were removed (to 7,116). Variable-level missingness was below 3% and assumed MAR; missing values were imputed using missForest. Outlier analyses indicated heavy tails for several socio-emotional indices; after testing scenarios, 5% trimming was applied, yielding a final analytic sample of 6,779. The dependent variable PVORT was constructed as the arithmetic mean of the ten PISA plausible values (PV1–PV10) and all predictors plus PVORT were re-standardized (z-scores) within the Türkiye subsample. Thirteen predictors were retained for all models for comparability.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Türkiye (15-year-olds) — Mathematics literacy (PVORT mean of 10 plausible values)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Stacking (GLMNET meta-learner): R² = 0.319 ± 0.042; RMSE = 0.777 ± 0.016; MAE = 0.633 ± 0.000. XGBoost: R² = 0.313 ± 0.041; RMSE = 0.781 ± 0.017; MAE = 0.636 ± 0.019. Random Forest: R² = 0.304 ± 0.045; RMSE = 0.786 ± 0.018; MAE = 0.641 ± 0.001. ANN: R² = 0.288 ± 0.048; RMSE = 0.795 ± 0.019; MAE = 0.653 ± 0.003. LASSO: R² = 0.273 ± 0.052; RMSE = 0.803 ± 0.020; MAE = 0.658 ± 0.000. MLR (OLS): R² = 0.270 ± 0.053; RMSE = 0.803 ± 0.021; MAE = 0.658 ± 0.000. Statistical tests: Friedman χ²(4)=33.04 (R²), 30.96 (RMSE), 26.40 (MAE), all p < .001; post hoc Wilcoxon indicates Stacking and XGBoost outperform linear approaches.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Türkiye mathematics literacy data (PVORT mean of 10 plausible values), the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS), mathematics self-efficacy, disciplinary climate, mathematics anxiety, and teacher support to predict mathematical literacy, finding that ensemble approaches outperformed linear models and that stacking achieved the highest out-of-fold performance (R² = 0.319; RMSE = 0.777; MAE = 0.633). This indicates that combining heterogeneous learners can improve predictive accuracy and stabilize error structures for identifying students at risk, while also reinforcing the policy relevance of socioeconomic inequality alongside student beliefs and classroom climate (with limitations because the study averages PVs and does not fully integrate PISA sampling weights into the ML pipeline, so results are predictive rather than causal).

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 Türkiye mathematics literacy for 15-year-olds using a dependent variable (PVORT) constructed as the arithmetic mean of the ten plausible values. After preprocessing (removing cases with >30% missingness, missForest imputation under MAR, 5% trimming of heavy-tailed indices, and re-standardizing within Türkiye), the authors train six predictive models—MLR (OLS), LASSO, Random Forest, XGBoost, a single-hidden-layer ANN, and a stacking ensemble—using the same 13 standardized predictors and 10-fold cross-validation with out-of-fold predictions. The stacking model performs best with R² = 0.319 (±0.042), RMSE = 0.777 (±0.016), and MAE = 0.633 (±0.000), followed by XGBoost (R² = 0.313) and Random Forest (R² = 0.304). Socioeconomic status (ESCS) is consistently the top predictor across methods, with mathematics self-efficacy and disciplinary climate also ranking highly. Limitations include averaging PVs instead of Rubin-type combination rules and incomplete integration of PISA complex sampling weights into the ML workflow, so findings support prediction and prioritization rather than causal claims.
